subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS-LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has not
been customaiy for the house to sit three times a day when the committees have not completed their work. The general rule has been that the work of the committees shall have been completed or practically completed before such a motion is adopted, for reasons which I think are fairly obvious. For instance, if the special commitee on electoral matters is to consider the measure that is now before it, lion, members who are associated
with me on that committee cannot be there and in the house at the same time. They would like to be in the house, in view of the legislation that is now before us. Under the circumstances I think the government should determine what legislation it will not proceed with, or that we should not sit three times a day unless there is a likelihood of our being able to conclude our sittings this week.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS-LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM
speechtext: I believe the committees generally have about concluded their work. It is quite true that one committee will have to sit again, but I imagine that hon. members of that committee might be prepared to accommodate each other and sit from ten to eleven o'clock in the morning if necessary. However, for some time past, all committees have been sitting more or less while the house has been in session. This may impose a slight additional burden, but I am inclined to think that it is one which will be accepted willingly by hon. members if there is a prospect of the house proroguing on Thursday of this week. From what I have been told by the whips I understand there is every reason to believe that we may be able to get through the remaining legislation without undue haste if we begin sittings in the morning. I think in any event it would be best to begin the sittings in the morning and if we find we cannot get through before July, continue them for whatever time thereafter may be desired by hon. members. I believe it accords with the general wish to have the house begin its morning sittings tomorrow.

speechtext:
From a perusal of press reports I notice that some municipalities are considering plans and ways and means of building houses which will cost from three to four thousand dollars, and are figuring 51952-270
on rentals varying from $25 to $35 a month. I am sure the minister does not contemplate either a cost of that extent or rentals of that variety, and a statement from the minister would do a great deal to clarify the situation in the country. These reports have given rise to criticism of the act and the intention of the government, it being stated that persons with incomes of $125 to $150 a month do not merit being subsidized either by reduction in taxation or by cheap money. So far as I am concerned, and I believe the house is in agreement, this measure is intended to benefit people whose monthly income varies from say sixty to ninety dollars or not more than a hundred dollars a month, and who have families to keep. The intention of the government is to assist such people in providing homes in which their families can be brought up as good Canadian citizens, not to subsidize persons whose incomes, as indicated in these press dispatches, are from $125 to 150 a month. If that view becomes prevalent, property owners in these centres will be opposed to the act and to any by-law which it may be necessary to submit to the burgesses for approval.

I do not want to labour the point, but it should be emphasized again and again that these groups are not entitled to the benefit of this act, nor should they by any stretch of the imagination think that they have the right to be subsidized by cheap money or reduced taxation. The benefits of the act should go to people of low incomes such as teamsters and those engaged in seasonal occupations

National Housing Act

As a matter of fact his suggestion is effected in section 15, paragraph (a), which provides that no family housing unit shall be leased to any family whose total family income is equal to or more than five times the economic rental of such family housing unit. I agree that the clause now before the committee might very well afford an additional opportunity for the governor in council to prevent any abuse of the kind to which my hon. friend has referred.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: There is a point here which should be made clear. I asked the Minister of Finance a question with regard to it the other day when we were discussing paragraph (b) of section 15, and the answer was not satisfactory. If a man and his family move into one of these flats, the man's total income being $900 and the rent $200, it may happen that a son of fourteen a few years later gets a job giving him a few dollars a week, and the total annual income may then be over $1,000. Does that family have to move? The son may be in residence in the flat but a short time and then move away. Are you going to cause the family the inconvenience of having to get out because their income exceeds the limit by a few dollars?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
The regulations should
cover the contingency the hon. member mentions. The regulations would normally set out the term of the lease and within that term it could very well be provided that no lessee should be obliged to vacate even if the family income should exceed that laid down as a qualification for the rental of family housing units. Apart from that, however, one must allow a certain degree of discretion in the drawing up of agreements with the municipalities concerned. speechtext:
I believe it is the taxation which is creating difficulty so far as housing is concerned. The decrease in the value of construction contracts in Canada has been particularly noticeable in certain years. I have before me construction figures in millions of dollars from the year 1927. They are as follows:
1927		$418,000,000
1928		 472,000,000
1929		 576,000,000
1930		 457,000,000
1931		 313,000,000
1932		 132.000,000
1933		 97,000,000
1934		 125,000.000
1935		 160.000,000
1936		 163,000,000
1937		 220,000,000
Hon. members will notice that there was a sharp drop in 1932, and an increase from 1934. In fact there has been a gradual increase since 1933, when the value of contracts reached its lowest point. Unemployment costs are going up and from year to year are adding to the
taxation. Many municipalities are behind in the replacement of their equipment, and now we are asking the people of Canada to enter into further private and public debt to the' extent of possibly another hundred million* dollars. We are giving them the assurance-that the government will pay one hundred per cent of the taxes in the first year, fifty per cent in the second year and twenty-five per cent in the third year, but what assurance have we that these people are going to be able to pay their taxes in the fourth year? I believe we would be dealing more equitably with the matter and would be taking action which would be more apt to reduce taxation for all concerned if we were to relieve the municipalities of unemployment costs and the heavy burden of unemployment relief. I am not opposed to giving assistance in the manner indicated in the bill, but I must point out that at the end of four years the people are-going to face increased taxation, without any assurance that they will be able to find the money with which to pay it. I would ask the minister to consider some means of reducing taxation in the municipalities other than that of simply paying taxes on a few houses.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: The answer to the hon. member's observations is that the measure does two things: in the first place, it provides for an immediate relief of taxation on new construction of the kind contemplated in this part of the bill. In the second place, it is designed to afford a further stimulus to the construction industry. In other words, it is to provide more employment. The more employment we have the less unemployment and relief we will have to contend with in the municipalities. The intention and hope is that the legislation will attack the problem at two points, namely, immediate relief from taxation for those who build under this part of the bill, and new employment in the construction trades and in general labour, thereby in due course reducing the incidence of unemployment relief in the municipalities.

speechtext: It would appear that, as Arthur Kitson says, this is like a prison gate which opens only inward. It is just a trap for some people. We encourage them to go ahead and to build so that we may relieve unemployment. But we relieve unemployment only temporarily. Then, back comes the unemployment. At the end of three or four years the taxpayer finds himself with the prison gates closed and no way of escape. He owes money that he will not be able to pay, and the result will be that the government will have the property thrown back on them.

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue, for Mr. Dunning) moved the second reading of Bill No. 160, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might perhaps at this stage state very briefly on behalf of the group with which I am associated that we are very glad indeed to see this legislation brought before the house, and we will do everything we can to facilitate its passage. The Montreal Gazette of May 30 last was good enough to state in its columns that "this is a victory for the

C.C.F., which has been urging complete nationalization." It went on to say that it was a triumph of no practical importance.
This measure can be of great practical importance. It depends on how the new Bank of Canada functions and to what extent it is made an instrument of public policy. I should like to think that just as in Sweden, New Zealand and other countries where the central bank is under national ownership and control, the Bank of Canada will play an important part in preventing booms on the upswing and deflationary depressions on the downswing. I believe that a central bank publicly owned and properly operated can do much in these directions.
As we look back over the years it will be found that the group with which I am associated has consistently advocated this reform. As early as May, 1922, for example, Mr. William Irvine, who was then a Labour member of this house, moved for the appointment of a committee to investigate the basis, function and control of financial credit. I read those debates at the time and have read them since, and as the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) suggests, the proposal at that time was met with ridicule.
In 1924 Mr. Robert Gardiner said:
I think the time is coming when we in Canada will demand that instead of banks being allowed to issue their own notes, they shall have a central bank operated by the government that will be responsible for the issuing of money.
In June, 1925, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) spoke on the nationalization of banking.
In April, 1926, Mr. Gardiner moved:
That in the opinion of this house the time has come for the establishment of a national system of banking.
In February, 1928, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre moved again for the establishment of a national system of banking.
In 1931 Mr. George Coote moved:
That a nationally owned central bank be established.
In 1932 Mr. Robert Gardiner moved, as a subamendment to the budget, for the nationalization of banking and currency.
In 1934 Mr. Lucas brought the matter forward, and later in the same year Mr. H. E. Spencer moved a budget amendment for the control of credit.
In 1935 Mr. Irvine moved-this was the last resolution on the subject that the U.F.A.- Labour group moved:
That all banking, including the central bank, be nationalized at once.

Bank of Canada
Coming down to 1936 we of this Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group fathered a similar resolution.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: So did ours.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I mention these facts because sometimes we and those associated with us are accused of advocating reforms and policies that are impossible of enactment or achievement, and yet over a period of years we often find that those policies which were met with ridicule at the beginning are found to be in the public interest as time goes on and find their place ultimately on the statute books of Canada.
To my mind this reform, for reform it is, and useful as it is, is not going to be found to be quite sufficient. We who have been advocating that the chartered banks of Canada should be brought under greater public control believe that this will ultimately take place. I realize of course that public opinion has to be moulded in order that such reforms may come about, and we shall not cease the educational work we are doing in relation to these matters until the commercial banks are brought under public control and public ownership as well; for, after all, the responsibility for directing most of the country's short term credit rests with the chartered or commercial banks. Their credit policy, as has been stated before, accentuates booms and depressions by easing credit during periods of prosperity and tightening it during periods of depression or deflation. Not only that, but I believe that their position at the present time tends towards the creation of monopolies of which banking is one. The fact that we have now a central bank which is going to be publicly owned and controlled is the bringing of one type of monopoly under public supervision, public control and, to some extent, public ownership. The chartered banks themselves through their interlocking directorates are very largely a part of the monopolistic set up of industry, and that is a matter which, if we are to make this central bank function, we shall have to consider very carefully in the days to come.
As I have so often said, I do not believe that the mere control of banking is the panacea which is going to cure all our economic and social ills. It is only one phase of a many sided problem. But I welcome this reform because it does bring nearer the time when we should be able to bring under control those economic forces which ultimately must minister to the common good. As I said in the debate on the budget, I believe that this
reform should be paralleled as quickly as possible by the setting up of a national investment board. A national securities board was recommended following the price spreads inquiry, and a comprehensive national securities board would do much to direct investments into safe and proper channels.
Just a few minutes ago we were discussing a bill to promote low-cost housing. That has been necessary largely because private enterprise has not entered into the field of low-cost housing, because of the risks and because the profits were not large enough. We have to find money for enterprises of that description. I believe that, with a nationally owned bank and a national securities board or investment board directing, first, the savings of the people, and, ultimately, the financial returns from all our own national industries and economic undertakings, we could do much to bring about improvements in housing and in the general conditions of the people.
This is near the close of the session. I do not wish to make a long speech. All I rose to do was to say that we are in approval of this legislation, which w'e have long advocated, and we hope that as the days go by the operations of this bank will be in the interests of Canada. It can be, as the Montreal Gazette said, of no consequence, or it can be of paramount importance to the people. That is very largely in the hands of the government and of this parliament. We wish to see the central bank operated, as central banks have been operated in New Zealand and Sweden, in accordance with the needs of the nation, for both the producers and the consumers. Thus we hope that the national bank will perform a great service to this dominion in the days to come.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I wish to make only a few remarks about this measure. Many spokesmen of the party represented by the group to our right, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, have been carrying on for the past two or three years a campaign of misrepresentation regarding the attitude of our group on this question. For instance, they have repeatedly stated that we voted against the nationalization of the Bank of Canada. Of course that is an absolute misstatement of fact. This is the first time a motion has been brought into parliament for this purpose. A motion was formerly brought in to give parliament greater powers of control, and we as a group voted solidly for that motion. On the other hand these speakers have stated that when a motion was introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to nationalize the Bank of Canada and the private banks of the country, we as a group voted against that motion. That statement is also an absolute misstatement of fact.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I rise to a point of
order. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Queleh) is not stating the fact. We have stated and do state that they officially spoke against the introduction of that motion. That, I think, is substantiated in Hansard.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I was referring to speakers of the party. I do not necessarily say it was said by members of this house. I said that these speakers have stressed the fact time and again throughout the country that we as a group voted against a motion which was introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar for the purpose of nationalizing the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. There is no truth in that statement. We did not vote against that motion. A recorded vote was never taken. Moreover, had a recorded vote been taken, a very large majority of the members of this group would have voted in favour of that motion. We have stressed over and over again that we do not regard nationalization as a question of major importance. What we regard as the most important point is the effective control of policy. We believe that the present policy of the banking system should be changed, because under the existing policy the amount of money in circulation does not necessarily have any relationship to the requirements

of the people. We desire a change to be brought about so that money shall be put into circulation to make the present physical demand of the people an effective demand against the production of the country.
What is the main purpose of this motion? Public ownership of the Bank of Canada just to save interest on one hundred thousand class A shares? That is desirable, but it does not really mean very much. On the other hand, was the resolution introduced chiefly to help out with the Saskatchewan election? It is strange that it was introduced about that time; it is strange that there was no notice of it in the speech from the throne. It is interesting to note the attitude on this question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1936. As recorded in Hansard at page 3S08, he stated as follows:
. . . and I repeat it now: I think the question of ownership is debatable, for reasons which appear in what I have said repeatedly in this house. I do not think the question of effective control is debatable. I think if you have effective public control it matters relatively little where the ownership rests, but if you have not effective public control then ownership in full may be desirable should it prove to be the only way to acquire it.
I would agree with that. The Prime Minister did not think ownership was absolutely essential. Why a change now? Is he convinced that we have not effective control? And if the Prime Minister is convinced that we have not, does he think for one minute that this measure will provide it? He said:
. . . ownership in full may be desirable should it prove to be the only way to acquire it.
And yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), speaking on February 28, 1938, as recorded in Hansard at page 891, stated:
. . . this parliament through instruments which it has created and which are now in operation does control currency and credit in Canada day by day, week by week and month by month.
That statement is definite. Then why this amendment? The Prime Minister said that ownership would be necessary only if control could not be acquired otherwise. It is interesting to note that shortly after that date the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking in Edmonton in the Edmonton East by-election, said on March 16:
"There are cries on all sides to change the banking system," said Mr. Gardiner. "Changes are being made, and I say the time cannot come too soon for me when the government has control over credit and currency in this country. I mean control entirely in the hands of the government of Canada. If no other party interferes with present legislation passed by the Liberal government, such control will be in effect in 1945."

Bank of Canada
The Minister of Finance, speaking on February 28, said that we had control; the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in Edmonton on March 16, said that we would not have it until 1945. There appears to be a great deal of confusion in the minds of members of the cabinet as to exactly what control means and whether or not this government has control.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: They are learning.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: They may be learning, but I say that this government has absolutely no control over the issue of currency and credit, and this amendment will not give it.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Vote against it.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
We are not going to vote against it; we will support it as a very small step in the right direction. I shall refer to that later on. It is interesting to note that while the Minister of Finance on February 28 said that we had control, nevertheless in his speech on March 8 he shows quite clearly that we have no effective control over the issue of currency and credit. Let me quote his words:
Mr. Dunning:	. . . We come back, then, to
the question whether the present volume of currency and credit in circulation in Canada is adequate for the needs of business and whether a further increase would be beneficial. It must first be understood that an increase in Bank of Canada note issue does not mean more notes in the hands or pockets of the public. Whatever medium be used for issuing the new currency or credit, such as the proposed one of financing the construction of public works, the central bank's notes would be immediately deposited with the chartered banks. An increase of, say $350,000,000 in chartered bank holdings of Bank of Canada notes would increase their cash reserves from the present figure of about $250,000,000 to $600,000,000, and their cash ratio from about ten per cent to roughly twenty-one per cent.
The sponsor of the suggestion contends that no inflation is intended or would result by thus increasing bank cash, so long as the gold cover of the Bank of Canada did not fall below the twenty-five per cent minimum. This factor, however, is not a test of inflation. If the banks use their increased cash in the normal way, as a basis for the extension of roughly ten times as much in loans to the public, or for the acquisition of ten times as much in investments, bank deposits would expand by approximately an equal amount until the cash ratio was brought down again to approximately ten per cent. This would mean an increase in bank deposits from the present level of about $2,387,000,000 to something like $0,000,000,000, or more than 2-6 times the level of December 31, 1929. Am I merely old fashioned or orthodox when I say that this would mean a colossal measure of inflation?
Let us suppose that the increase in the amount of money adequately to meet the needs of business is 8350,000,000. Then, as
the minister points out, there will be the danger that the chartered banks may expand this to $3,500,000,000, thereby causing inflation. They may not do so, but on the other hand they may. How, then, can the minister possibly claim that we have effective control? As I pointed out on March 14, the kind of control that we have at the present time is similar to the sort of control that we might have over a high-powered car with a defective steering gear. It would be absolutely impossible to hold it on a given course because the reaction to any turn of the wheel might be exaggerated.
This amendment does not increase control, and therefore I urge that the Bank Act be amended so as to compel the chartered banks to maintain 100 per cent cash reserve against checking deposits. This reserve might be made available by the government through the national bank purchasing from the chartered banks a sufficient quantity of government securities to provide that backing. Then the chartered banks henceforth would be compelled to maintain permanently a cash reserve of 100 per cent against their demand deposits. The result would be a great reduction in the national debt followed by a reduction in taxation. The Minister of Finance speaking some time ago said, I believe, that 43 per cent of all taxation went towards the payment of interest. The result would be 100 per cent control over the issue of currency and credit. The amount of money required in circulation would be decided by the Bank of Canada and so regulated. Money required for public works would be issued by the Bank of Canada without danger of inflationary action on the part of the chartered banks.
This proposal has been endorsed by prominent men who have made an exhaustive study of the question of money such as Professor Irving Fisher, Professor Soddy, and Robert Hemphil, former credit manager of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, and many eminent bankers throughout the United States. On the other hand it has been said that the banks could not operate on this basis because it would mean a great curtailment of their profits. But, as has been pointed out on former occasions in this house, the profits of the banks at the present time are excessive, and their expenditures on many lines are extravagant. When we consider the tremendous privileges the chartered banks enjoy, I would say that they are not rendering to the people the service they have a right to demand. I have in mind the closing of many branches throughout western Canada in the past nine
Bank of Canada

or ten years, and more recently one might describe their action as being tantamount to blackmail; for they have been using their power to compel or persuade the people to demand from the government that certain legislation shall be annulled under the threat that if such action is not taken they will close certain branches in Alberta. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) the other day gave a good talk on this matter, pointing out that the banks were trying to exercise a form of dictatorship. I do not think such a condition is desirable in a so-called democratic country. So I would say that if the chartered banks refuse to cooperate on that basis, the whole banking system should be nationalized.
There are many other things one might discuss, but as we are trying to finish the session by the end of the month I shall merely say that in our opinion the main monetary policy of this government should be to put in the hands of the people sufficient money to make the present physical demand of the people into an effective demand against the production of the country, and as that production increases, to see that the ability of the people to procure that production shall be increased in like degree. While we in this corner intend to support the motion as a step in the right direction, we point out that it is absolutely valueless for the purpose of giving the government effective control over the issue of currency and credit.

speechtext:
promptly develop serious results. The explanation involves a big story, which I do not intend to give, but I can open it out and leave the details to the imaginations of hon. members. There is a system, albeit a bastard one, of social credit, already at work within our economy. It constitutes the whole structure of the wages of money. For example, a light and power company is producing electricity and can sell it at a price much less than is now being paid. But a large section of the citizens of the country are already, in consideration of money introduced, receiving all or nearly all of the social credit which it is possible for that particular light and power company to contribute; and, therefore, the destruction of its capital structure must be insisted upon, or it must be left out of the social credit plan for the country. This is most serious; for practically all businesses and all industries are wedded to this admittedly bastard form of social credit, and the dividends already being distributed to the citizens of the country leave no profits on which the social credit of my hon. friends may be based.
It is no lessening of the force of this argument to observe that the idea that the social credits of which I have spoken are raggedly and quite unfairly distributed to the citizens, and the instances are not few which demonstrate that the actual worker is robbed of his wages to support this peculiar social credit structure.
Upon the unquestioned force of this argument I declare that the social credit of the hon. members cannot possibly be imposed upon the present economy, not only because there is no place for it that is not already filled, but because of its very nature, if it is to be conceived of as a purely concocted panacea of the economic ills which flesh is heir to. Every citizen who can produce, every citizen who would produce if opportunity afforded and every citizen who is accepted by the citizenry as a non-producer, whether by grace or by reason of personal incompetence or incapacity-and these categories are intended to include the whole of the citizenry-are fully entitled to the benefit of a pure social credit. It can only be developed, however, in those fields of our economic activity where the profits of production are developed for the benefit of the whole citizenry. This represents pro tanto the advantages of a socialist economy, and I therefore assert that only in some form of socialism in our economy can we look for social credit to function properly.
I am prepared at this stage of my review of the situation to declare that the irresistible forces of our civilization are driving us rapidly

into a form of national economy which will grant first one and then another of our productive and distributive functions for the unrestricted benefit of the citizens as a whole. Only in such cases can social credit ever be adequately established, and by the same token only in such cases can socialism ever become available to advance the condition of our people.
And this will be true just as certainly if, unhappily, civil revolution be invoked to bring it about; for revolution in itself can and will accomplish nothing. It is what is built on the ruins of a revolution which will determine the future of the unlucky people who have to pass through it. And, too, often in such case the reconstruction of society proceeds haltingly because of the irrevocable and irrecoverable loss of those elements of government which, by virtue of their essential worth, constituted the cementing properties of the government now overthrown, while of necessity new cementing elements will take a long time to accrete, and thus properly to perform their function.
It may still be advanced that I have not yet fully covered the phase of the problem developed by the social credit formula which proposes to introduce to our economy nonrepayable sums at the free disposal of every citizen. I am urging that in effect all I have said covers this matter. But let me observe that the whole financial system of the country in its multifarious ramifications always adjusts itself and seeks its own level, and does so by the age-old governing rule of debit and credit. It is tied definitely at the one end to the consumer, and at the other end to the producer. The social credit formula now introduces a medium of exchange which is tied only at the producer end and which leaves the consumer end floating free. It is through or by this free floating end that the nonrepayable dividend created out of nothing by the social credit government will flow into the otherwise balanced, though admittedly badly adjusted, economy. This will create a condition never before practised, and it must be studied with great care.
For our study we can think of the $25 per month proposed to be given as social credit to every citizen of Alberta. Of course we must admit and agree that, when given, that sum must, either at the outset or later, be related definitely and scientifically to the spread between the cost of production and the ability to purchase within that province. In effect each Alberta citizen is made, by the free flowing ink of the pen of a ready writer, richer by $300 per annum. Let us sense the repercussions. First, of course the

Bank of Canada
spread between the cost of production and the price of purchase will vary considerably with every product. Second, of course the citizens will be neither constant nor consistent in their unrestricted choice of the products purchased. Therefore, I unhesitatingly declare that it will be practically impossible to equate these inconstant elements. No arbitrary monthly payment of money to citizen purchasers will in itself justify or equate a scientifically ascertained just price for the above cogent reasons. However, my social credit friends may believe the plan to be really practical; I do not.
I describe given money and non-repayable dividends as being inferior to earned money and, therefore, liable to the vagaries of inferior money in a financial system, in spite of the fact that in use it will be undiscoverable from the ordinary money of the economy. I assert that there is grave danger to an existing financial structure in padding it with an inferior currency. All hon. members will sense the concern with which the manufacturer will view the new situation presented by a supposedly easy market for his products when he remembers how he pared down his cost of production and profit margins in order to satisfy the market before the new credit was introduced. All hon. members will sense the chagrin of workers who accepted lower wages to help their employers meet the competitive market when they discover the products on which they worked entering an easy market. The inevitable result in both cases will be a definite readjustment of prices until an equitable condition obtains for worker and manufacturer alike. This equitable condition will not be reached without a very much increased distribution of so-called dividends.
There is another highly important problem. Hon. members know that the S25 per month will represent pin-money to one citizen, while to another it will represent almost an adequate living allowance. And so we beat the devil around the stump, and we turn to the arguments first cited for this problem. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is so earnest in his efforts to awaken the people and the government to the advantages of both to be discovered in the newer financial economy that I dislike finding myself in disagreement with him. However, I am unable to travel with him in his statements as recorded on page 4197, column 1, paragraph 2, of Hansard, for the following reasons. If an individual banking institution finds to-day that it requires 10 per cent of its total deposits as till money for the safe and reasonable conduct of its business, no legislation of the government can change the bank's empiric findings. The
Bank of Canada, however, by virtue of section 27 of the Bank of Canada Act, 1934, and also subsection 4 of section 59 of the Bank Act, 1934, has assumed the guardianship and sufficiency of till moneys and demands that 5 per cent of all deposit liabilities shall be in either a Bank of Canada deposit account or in Bank of Canada notes, which means that the said 5 per cent must be in such liquid condition as the Bank of Canada might be legally accountable, answerable and responsible for. A reference to the liquid reserves with which the chartered banks can conduct their business would reveal the fallacy that they build up 8100 of loan deposits from $5 of Bank of Canada notes.
Further, a close study of section 26 of the Bank of Canada Act, 1934, will reveal the dangers attending any banking practice which would avail of all the legal limits assigned to it. There is an interesting point in the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, as reported' in Hansard at page 4068, column 1, paragraph 2. This reads:
. . . but I do commend to the Prime Minister and his government serious and fair consideration of my statement to-night that the major weapons of control, by which we were told the government through the Bank of Canada would regulate the volume of currency and credit in the interests of the economic life of the nation, are not effective; because I am satisfied that the majority of the members of the government will not permit that statement to go unchallenged, if my conclusions, from the facts I have analysed to-night, are justified and correct.
On this I make vigorously this important observation. The legally established functions of the Bank of Canada do appear to have strengthened the financial structure of the country to resist the destructive force of an impending recession. But the other side of the picture is not equally clear. The ability of the central bank to place large funds at the disposal of the banks does not necessarily bring about a stimulus to flagging business or flagging industry. Economists of every kind will have to learn that in our present economy of practical plenty the stimulus will have to be applied to the individual citizen. Stimulate the individual who wants something which his country has made it possible for him to obtain, and we shall hear no more of the frustrations of poverty; we shall hear no more of unemployment; we shall begin to make of our country the glorious dwelling place it is capable of becoming.
Pierpont Morgan, the banker, told the commission which inquired into the conditions surrounding the collapse of 1929 that he would not hesitate to loan S5.000 to any man whom he believed honest and capable, without consideration of security. In essence this
Bank of Canada

is done frequently by bankers. I submit that this leads us logically in the direction of economic security for our people, and points the way by which it can be developed. While absence of sufficient money will bring about a recession of business, a pentitude of it in the hands of bankers or the central bank will not act per contra. If every citizen in Canada were rich but miserly, our business would be relatively small; nevertheless, if every citizen in Canada were poor, but could be persuaded that his social security was being established and guaranteed by the government, his economic wants could be gradually built up until he reached a more just and reasonable distribution of the productive and distributive capacity of our wonderful country.
What, then, is my aim and to what end should we mould the legal functions of the Bank of Canada? The essentials of life in this or any country are food, shelter and clothing.
There is in Canada an average w'age. This average wage represents the general standard of achievement of our citizens. Of this average wage, food, shelter and clothing each demand a definite percentage which varies only fractionally within well-defined limits. These are the pegs upon which we can hang the social security of our people.
For this reason I say that it is now possible to extend the operations of our banking system through the functions of the Bank of Canada, widened for that purpose, so as to provide a series of automatically recurring credits to every citizen of our country, which credits shall become loans as they are availed of and only for the amount availed of. Every such loan will be repayable to the country in one form or another, and, what is most important, such credits and loans will be related to and used only for one branch of our economic necessities at a time until it has justified its existence and completely proven its practicability.
In this manner, by an internal currency, can we quickly bring to everyone according to his need, and demand from everyone his share. Employment will increase at once. Initiative will in no sense be destroyed, and, as I have said, an economic standard can be automatically raised in scientific adjustment to the material development of the country.
Such credits introduced gradually and scientifically will differ altogether from the Aberhart and Douglas conceptions, and will be freed basically from the faults already elaborated.
It will revolutionize the present system, not by overthrowing it but by bringing to it

a commercial understanding which recognizes its essential values and the complexities of its structure, and it will be definitely coordinated to it.
It will be tied at both ends-tied to the producer and tied to the consumer alike- and will carry the unquestioned and inescapable responsibility of a repayable loan.
It will be accepted freely by all honest citizens, and the dishonest orfes will very quickly learn their lesson when deprived of its blessings. All this lies within the possible use to which we can bring our Bank of Canada, and I say this after much thought and after study of the trend of financial and industrial thought and practice everywhere. When the opportunity occurs in which I may extend my observations along this line, it will be with a developed plan, the outcome of much careful study and preparation.
No one can boast happily of his country unless he has himself enabled it to be and to become the provider of adequate and continuous sustenance to every citizen, male or female, adult or of tender years-unless he has assisted to bring to his people a secure existence in the midst of its plenty.
Finally, creation is an unhappy word to use to explain the physical functions of banking or credit or any other expression of our economy. Unless we produce and distribute at a profit by human effort, we must produce and distribute at a loss, and that way lie inefficiency, chaos and despair, notwithstanding all the claims of orthodox socialists for the elimination of the price system. It will eliminate itself when the right time and the right social conditions come together, and we have it in our power to make the Bank of Canada speed that happy day.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a very great pity that the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) chose this time, when we are all anxious to close this session, to precipitate a discussion on the principles of social credit after he has sat here for five months during almost every day of which he might have debated the matter.
I am going to present my case straightforwardly to the house and to those who read Hansard. We do not wish to protract this session, and consequently are not at this time going to go into a discussion of the details of social credit, but if the hon. member will bring his ideas up next session we shall deal with them until there will not be powder left of them.
I am just going to read three or four quotations which need to go into Hansard because

Bank of Canada
they are vital, and then I shall turn for a very brief period to a discussion of the Bank of Canada.
The other day the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) gave a quotation which I am going to read into Hansard again because of its bearing on what the hon. member for Nanaimo has said. It is this:
The first important thing to bear in mind is this, that money can be created.
The chief reason why the social crediters have used the banks as an illustration of the creation of money is simply to show that this can be done.
I am going to read now the quotation from John Maynard Keynes as given the other day on page 4194 of Hansard by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. If the hon. member for Nanaimo wishes to question Mr. Keynes on this matter, he is at liberty to do so. Mr. Keynes said:
The creation of legal tender has been and is a government's ultimate reserve; and no state is likely to decree its own bankruptcy or its own downfall so long as this instrument remains at hand unused.
Thus we accept Mr. McKenna's contention that an expansion of credit is the key to the situation. But we conclude that if whilst an increased volume of bank credits is probably a sine qua non of increased employment, a program of home investment which will absorb this increase is a sine qua non of the same expansion of credit.
All I wish to say this afternoon in the contribution I desire to make to this debate is included in that statement. All one has to do is to enlarge upon it. Again, as reported at page 4195 of Hansard the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard gave this quotation from the Right Hon. Mr. McKenna's report to his bank:
The quantity of our money is no longer governed by the fortuitous supply of gold and the degree to which hoarding is practised by central banks and others. The quantity of money is subject now to pure management with first regards to the needs of commerce and industry.
That again expresses the whole contention of the monetary reformers and the whole contention of the social credit movement, because it is a movement of monetary reformers.
Again, as reported on the same page of Hansard, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard quoted from the London Economist of May 21, 1938:
There are distinct signs that the policy of cheap plentiful credit-
The hon. member for Nanaimo will notice that the word " credit " is used there.
-is being continued and intensified so as to combat the recession, and also so as to facilitate the financing of rearmament.
May I break in there to point out that if credit is sufficiently sound money to finance rearmament, it will finance dividends at any time.

speechtext:
The quotation from the London Economist continued:
Such a deduction is not at variance with the occasional reaffirmations of monetary policy which from time to time have emerged from official quarters.
I am going to read again from an address by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna on January 29, 1936, in the following words:
We learned that a shortage of money may be just as vicious in its effects as an excess. It is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money, for otherwise prices will fall, business will stagnate, and the growing productive capacity will be unused. For money to be thoroughly sound, there must be enough of it to finance an ordinary growing volume of trade, yet not so much as to give rise to an inflationary movement of prices.
The whole social credit idea is involved in that statement. Let me draw attention particularly to these words:
It is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money.
Too frequently men lose sight of the fact that we are in an age of abundance in which we are producing more goods than we are now able to sell, and in which we are capable of producing many more goods than we are now producing. Consequently, it is abundantly manifest that our productivity has increased. The social credit contention is that at the present time there is no adequate device, no adequate government control, by means of which that increase of money is made which is necessary as a result of the increased productivity; and even if the amount of money is increased, there exists at the present time no means whereby that money can be put into circulation in such a way as to enable the people who need the goods to buy the goods; consequently, to enable the people who have the goods for sale, to sell the goods. When the hon. member for Nanaimo

Bank of Canada

or any other man in Canada thinks he can argue that away, he is welcome to try it next session.
It is extremely necessary that I should not take very much time, and I am going to leave that, letting anyone who wishes to read it, do so. I am going to give another extract, from an article in the London Times of January 30, 1936, by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, at page 23:
Additional currency, however, can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers, without reference to the central bank's holdings of gold. Thus the nineteenth century, which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, . . .
He is manifestly referring there to credit.
. . . brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
The chief contention, apparently, which the hon. member for Nanaimo was making was that social crediters were running along unsound lines in contending that governments can create money and that the amount of money they can create depends upon the country's productivity. That quotation strongly supports our case. After you have created money, it is simply a matter of deciding how you are going to use it.
May I now turn to a consideration of the bill? The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has expressed our opinion as a group. We are going to support this measure, but our views in large measure agree with those recently expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Unless this Bank of Canada is correctly used, it is not going to do us the good that we hope it will do. Those people who have persuaded themselves that the mere ownership of the bank by the dominion government is going to solve their ills, are labouring under a delusion. Consequently it becomes extremely necessary to point this out at this stage. This bill is a step in the right direction, so we are going to support it.
May I hasten to say that we have no means of determining what the government are going to do with this bank. I assume they are going to use it wisely. I have no doubt about that; so I am not applying any criticism; I am merely pointing out the reason why I intend to support this measure.
There are two functions formerly performed by private persons which, on account of the rapid oncoming of the age of plenty, they are no longer disposed to undertake. The government, therefore, if disaster is to be avoided, must be prepared to supplement both of these functions. The first is that of capital
fMr. Blackmore.]
being invested in new concerns, factories and the like. Since 1929 capital has literally gone on strike; it appears no longer available or free to invest in new enterprises to produce goods. The banks would seem increasingly indisposed to lend money for those purposes. The other day, while we were quietly discussing this matter, I asked a man this question, "If you were a banker, would you lend money to go into sheep?" "Why," he said, "I should say not." I said, "Why would you not?" He stopped and thought about it for quite a little while. I intended he should. "Now," I said to him, "I am going to turn right around and ask you this question: "If you were a shrewd, intelligent farmer, would you borrow money with which to go into sheep?" He thought a very few minutes and finally said, "I do not think I would." "Now," I said, "will you tell me why, in both cases? And when you get done telling me why, you will be ready to consider the proposals which I have." I will state briefly what we arrived at after about fifteen minutes. "Well," he said, "if I were a banker I would not lend money because I would be afraid I would not be able to get it back." I said, "Why?" "Because," he said, "the farmer would not be able to sell his goods." "Very well," I said, "your trouble is selling your goods. And that is the reason why the farmer will not take the money. Then your difficulty is concentrated on the question of consumption."
We can talk all we like about "confidence." President Roosevelt, I am told, spent a good deal of time the other night talking about it. People say it is because a certain government is not in; it is because of this, that and the other, that confidence is lacking. As long as they continue to have that idea, they will labour under a delusion, because the reason for the lack of confidence is that men fear they cannot sell. Capital, I say, has gone on a sort of sit-down strike since 1929. May I cite some figures which I found the other day in a most interesting bank letter? In the United States the figures of new corporate financing of-late years are as follows:
Year	Amount
1928		$5,500,000,000
1929		 8,000,000,000
1933	 180,000,000
1935		 400,000,000
1936		 1,200,000,000
1937	 1,500,000,000
Many people tried in 1937 to persuade themselves that we were back to the 1929 level. All we need to do is just glance at the two figures. In 1929 United States business men invested $8,000,000,000 in new corporate financing. In 1937 they invested $1,500,000,000.

Bank of Canada
What we ask is this: What is the matter? Well, it is abundantly clear, is it not, that capital has gone on strike? The question for us to determine, therefore, is why and how we can overcome the difficulty. That very small figure in 1937 is the more striking when we remember that during all the years of the depression there has been insufficient expenditure of capital in new corporate financing. The result has been that there must have developed a distinct deficiency in capital production, a distinct lack of factories; notwithstanding that stimulus, however, there is no tendency whatever to pick that up by anything like an adequate expenditure. There is no tendency to make up the loss. How is that loss to be made up? That is the problem which faces the United States, and it faces Canada and. indeed, all the civilized nations of the world.
We do not need to argue about if's and but's, about the A plus B theorem or anything of that sort. There are the facts and they must be faced. What did the United States do to make up the loss? There are many people who are finding fault with Mr. Roosevelt's extravagant spending program, but these people never for a moment undertake to show how he could solve the problem without that spending. They do not realize that unless he can get that money without borrowing, then his nation is doomed, but they cannot see how he can get along without spending money. Social credit puts its finger on that problem. It says: There is your problem; you simply must have money, and if you cannot get it without borrowing or without taxation, then you might as well close up and get ready for your funeral, because it is coming and no amount of sneering or levity will dispose of the situation.
When, therefore, people say that we are not keeping our eyes on reality they are simply deceiving themselves; that is all. In 1932 in the United States the government went into debt about $3,000,000,000 distributing the money in every direction, in relief, and for every kind of project which would enable them to put the money out so that people could buy goods that industry wanted to produce and sell. Every year from that time forward until 1936 they spent a similar amount. In 1936 they spent $4,400,000,000, with the soldiers' bonus, and the money was expended in their WPA and CCC projects and in a great many other ways, all designed to put money right into the hands of the needy people in order that goods might be sold to the greatest advantage. Anyone can see in that program a dividend, though a very crude
51952-271^
sort of dividend. It is not scientific at all, but it is there. In 1937 they cut down this $4,400,000,000 to about $1,500,000,000, apparently because in the United States uninformed people behind Roosevelt began to clamour so vociferously for retrenchment, the balancing of the budget and all that sort of thing that the pressure exerted upon him was more than he could resist. The result was that he cut down the amount he was spending, and, behold, a recession. It may be said that the recession did not come because of that, but that would be something very difficult to prove. You notice that confidence is picking up and prices are rising as soon as a great amount of money goes out; and those who read the press in the last two or three days have read of Roosevelt's intention to rush recovery with $3,000,000,000. It means only one thing. They have discovered that one way out of the depression is by government spending of money.
If that $3,000,000,000 is being created in the United States by the banking systems, and if it could just as well be created by the government, then why not? That is a vital question which faces us as practical Canadian statesmen. Let me read what the Royal Bank of Canada says after a fine review. This is from the Royal Bank of Canada's letter of October, 1937:
Unless private expenditures of a capital nature can be stimulated it would seem that the, government will be compelled to increase its spending, or as an alternative, to permit a decline in national income.
The same applies to Great Britain. Most of us were interested in a certain powerful movement that took place over in Great Britain this year. I understand that a resolution was passed calling upon the government to declare what they were going to do in case the rearmament program ceased. The same question can be asked in Canada. What has the British government done? It has spent vast sums on rearmament, vast sums on rehousing, vast sums in divers social services and so on and so on, with the result that there is apparent recovery and prosperity, and those who are only superficial enough imagine that good times are coming back. But it is quite obvious that this is not so- obvious to those who read the words of people who are best informed.
I have said enough about the sit-down strike of investors. Now I will turn to the walk-out of consumers. They have quit buying; they have been compelled to, and the result is stagnation. The government must finance consumption. These measures which the United States has been adopting, the

Bank oj Canada
measures which Great Britain has been adopting, are all designed to finance both production and consumption. In my opinion the Bank of Canada must definitely and positively aim at two things. In the first place it must be prepared, by machinery which it will set up by and by, to finance production. The hon. member for Nanaimo began to talk a great deal of wisdom toward the end of his speech when he spoke about spending money to produce. That proposal is sound. May I say with regard to this good man that he is one of the best students I have ever met, and one of the most earnest men. I do not hold it against him that he does not see eye to eye with me on social credit; the day will come when he will; for the simple reason that the ideas, whether you call them social credit or not, are sound inasmuch as they go to the basis of the difficulty which confronts us.
Since it is necessary that we finance both consumption and production, we can readily appreciate what the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) felt the other day in a very fine outburst towards one of the greatest and most important utilities in our country, the utility of banking. We can understand why he implied-he did not exactly say it- that you should not allow a particular bank to go out of a certain little community. "Well," the banker pleads, "we are losing money." " Never mind whether you are losing money or not, you cannot destroy me and the community," he replies. Read his fine words, and remember the honour and respect which are universally accorded to that man, and the long practical experience he has had. He is not one who can be called an impossible idealist or a dreamer. He rises in his place in this house demanding exactly what the people of Alberta demand, namely, that the function of banking shall be subjected to an adequate measure of government control to prevent disaster from coming to the people. How well the hon. member expressed it. Perhaps, without violating the rules of the house, I might read one or two of his expressions. On page 4177 of Hansard for June 23 he is reported as saying:
Why should a man have his whole life work interfered with by a ruthless bank outsider who knows nothing and apparently cares less about the rural areas of the country? Is it any wonder I am furious and indignant? And then there is no redress.
Those might be the words of the province of Alberta; that is exactly the way we feel, and Saskatchewan, Ontario and every other province will feel that very thing after a while.

All that is necessary is to realize that banking is a public utility. Now consider his words as reported at page 4178:
If the banks will not correct this situation, what am I going to do?
Alberta is as it were speaking.
I am going to suggest to the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and all the government, that they take into careful consideration the desirability of having a board of bank commissioners, so that when a bronco banker like this one breaks out, a snub twitch or a lariat can be put on him. Do you think Canadians should have to submit to such tyranny? I do not. I would be ashamed to think that Canada had degenerated to that extent.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are exactly the views of Alberta. Yet some hon. members talk about Alberta being in open rebellion against Ottawa, and all that sort of thing; and say that the acts which Alberta passed in order to enable her to struggle against that very situation and bring it under some sort of control have to be disallowed immediately, with no redress from Ottawa whatsoever. The province is left to fight its way, just as this poor man and that little community where he lives. As soon as we as Canadians come to realize that Alberta, and men like the hon. member for Melville, are fighting for a real right, people will stop all this nonsensical talk.
I turn again to the policy of the Bank of Canada. My group have said time and again in this house that it is the policy of the bank which counts. Ownership is good, but you must have a right policy. You must recognize first that it is a public utility. After recognizing that, you will begin to be prepared to finance consumption; for example by pensions to the aged, to the blind, to the sick and incapacitated, to widows, mothers, orphans; greater and greater. Why? Simply because that is a means of financing consumption. You put the money into the hands of the people who wish to spend it, and who therefore will. The result is to develop markets to a fair degree. We shall follow that up with state medicine, state dentistry, and money for things which will tend to remove from the people the terrible burden they are now bearing. We are doing the most stupid things imaginable. One need only look at people who are raising families of five or six children. Do we want those families? Surely we do. But we place on them the burden of the sales tax, the burden of medicine, dentistry-one could go on and enumerate the great number of abuses as a result of which we put the burden on the very people who ought not to be bearing it-and we say that all is well. It is strange that

Bank of Canada
people all over the earth except Anglo-Saxons are able to see these injustices. But we shall see them by and by. Then we shall use this new state-created money in the reduction of prices; we shall subsidize consumers. It sounds silly, but is it? It is the common sense thing to do. Then we shall not be far away from dividends for all. It will all be paid for by the creation of new money. Let me revert to a quotation from Right Hon. Reginald McKenna in January, 1936:
Additional currency, however, can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers. . . .
It is additional currency, not old currency; it is not taxed from anyone; it is not borrowed from anyone.
My time has expired. I have already talked much longer than I had intended. I shall close with a little quotation which I think the longer hon. members consider, the more meaning they will find it has. It is from page 99 of Stuart Chase's book, Government in Business, quoting Arthur H. Adams, in the Key Ratio to Balance, published in the American Federationist of November, 1934:
The unbalance we have reached this time is so big that natural or automatic restoration of balance, or recovery, cannot occur. The buying power of all consumer goods workers in the United States-
And the same is true of Canada, of course.
*

needs to be raised about 35 per cent on the average, and with no increase in their producing power, before an intelligent man should even hope for business to become self-sustaining at normal levels.
That, too, is the situation which Canada faces. The Bank of Canada must be used for (he working out of the policy, first, of financing production, and second, of financing consumption.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock. BANK OF CANADA

Perhaps I had better say what I have to say at this time, because the title involves the whole question I wish to discuss. When the resolution was before the house I made such observations as I thought necessary with respect to the general principle of the measure. I endeavoured to point out that it is rather a commentary on our institutions that in 1936 we should have adopted what was regarded by the minister at that time as being the best possible method of effectuating public control over the Bank of Canada. When I heard him say the other evening that he still thought that this was so, but that the measure now before the committee was being put forward for the purpose of eliminating and removing criticism of the bank, I realized that while the reason is in itself sound, it is difficult to appreciate it in its entirety. I am afraid that the pressure of a near-by election had about as much to do with the matter as the public discussion as to the methods of the measure itself.
But there are two or three matters which I think might be considered to be of some importance. When I was in Australia I looked into the question of the Commonwealth Bank, and the conditions under which it was operated. It came into being without capital at all, borrowed a few pounds, relatively, from the government, and started into business. In 1937 a royal commission which was appointed in 1935-36 made a report, and with respect to the Commonwealth Bank they made the following recommendations which I think are of some importance:
1.	The governor should be chairman of the board by virtue of his office and should possess qualifications and receive a salary commensurate with the importance of the office. The appointment of the governor should not be made on the basis of seniority nor is it even essential that he should already be in the service of the bank.
2.	The six directors other than the governor and the secretary to the treasury should be appointed for a term of six years instead of seven as at present, one should retire each year, and be eligible for reappointment, but provision should be made that no director shall continue to hold office after reaching the age of 70.
3.	The limitation on the field of choice of directors in section II (2) (b) of the act should be removed. The members of the board should be selected for capacity and diversity of experience and contact, and not as representatives of special interests.
4.	The "Commonwealth Bank Act 1911-32," section 12B, which provides that there "shall be" *a board of advice in London, should be made permissive. This board is not at present constituted, and there seems to be no nceessity-for such a board in present circumstances.
Bank of Canada

Our new board will be thirteen in number. There are eleven to be appointed; the governor makes the twelfth, and the minister or his representative we will say, makes the thirteenth.

I said about 8, and the minister now tells me it has not been below 8-6 per cent in the last ten years. The only question that confronts us is: How can we make this bank more useful to the Canadian people and more responsive to their needs and necessities? There was a statement, which I think originated with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, as to public credit. If I remember rightly, this was adopted practically as a slogan by the government during
Bank of Canada

the election of 1935. This had to do with the utilization of the bank to the greatest possible extent in service to the people. But when it is suggested that the bank can make credit, there have to be conditions that permit of credit being made. The difficulty is that these conditions have not arisen in this country. Until they arise there is only one thing can be done-and the Minister of Finance made it perfectly clear that he at least was not prepared to do that-and that is by statutory enactment to provide what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) said would be done after the last election, namely, to issue paper money in relation to the gold reserve that is in the bank, which would permit hundreds of millions of dollars being issued. A portion of that money, he said, would be used to liquidate the national debt, and a portion used for other purposes. That has not been done although, remember, it was done in this country once. In 1915 we passed a statute legalizing the acts that had been done by the government of 1914. We issued $26,000,000 of Dominion of Canada bills, $10,000,000 of which had nothing behind them, $10,000,000 had behind them Canadian Northern securities which were worthless, and $6,000,000 had Grand Trunk Pacific securities behind them which were also worthless, and that $26,000,000 you will find referred to in chapter 4 of the statutes of 1915, where you will find these words; I shall not take time to read it all:
Whereas for the purposes set forth in orders in council of date the fifth day of September, 1914	(P.C. 2326), the twenty-sixth day of
September, 1914 (P.C. 2451), the twenty-fourth day of October, 1914	(P.C. 2671), and the
twentieth day of November, 1914 (P.C. 2922), and pursuant to said orders, advances to the amount of six million dollars ($6,000,000) in the form of an issue of dominion notes were made to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, against a pledge by the company of its guaranteed securities issued in pursuance of the provisions of the Grand Trunk Pacific Guarantee Act, 1914, by placing the sums so advanced to the credit of the Minister of Finance for payment out under the provisions of the deed of trust securing the issue of these securities;
And whereas pursuant to an order in council of date the second day of November, 1914 (P.C. 2750), dominion notes to the amount of ten million dollars ($10,000,000) were issued, in order that certain obligations of Canada might be met as they matured;
And whereas with respect to the greater part of these issues of dominion notes security in the form required by section 5 of the Dominion Notes Act 1914 was not held-

That was covered by the expansion of dominion note issues. But this was covered by the issue of notes by the dominion to liquidate three obligations: one to the Canadian Northern, one to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the other to the nation generally; one being for $10,000,000, one being for $6,000000, and the other being for $10,000,000. The other $20,000,000 stands on a somewhat different basis because the gold coverage was used for the purposes of protecting that issue. It was in order to avoid any discussion of that, that I referred to this particular statute. The hon. gentleman will realize that the gold coverage was behind the $20,000,000. The first recital deals with the $10,000,000 to the Canadian Northern, and that is validated by the legislation.
It is within the knowledge of all the members of this committee that if a bank found itself in need of cash it deposited with the Minister of Finance certain securities which it held, and the Minister of Finance handed out to that bank Dominion of Canada notes. For this accommodation the bank paid certain interest rates, sometimes 31 per cent, sometimes 4 per cent and sometimes 2i per cent. That issue of dominion notes was not protected by metallic coverage. That had nothing to do with it. It was only a temporary advance, and it will be observed that it was supported only by the securities which were deposited with the Minister of Finance for the purpose of enabling the advance to be made.

speechtext: Would it be a rediscount operation?

maintopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: The hon. member has anticipated what I was going to say. That we did not continue. It will be remembered that Sir Thomas White, in his dissenting opinion from the conclusions of the royal commission, said that that was quite ample for our purposes, but the bulk of professional as well as lay opinion was that that was not an easy or a safe way to carry on our operations. I use the word "safe," not from the standpoint of financial stability but as indicating a safe, sound way in which to carry on.

maintopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: To complete the picture which the right hon. gentleman is giving, will he tell us how the issue of $26,000,000 was finally withdrawn from circulation?

maintopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, it was not withdrawn from circulation. It was covered by the statute passed during the regime of the late government wihen we dealt with the note act and the legal tender act

Bank of Canada
and the coverage act after the conference of 1933, when 25 per cent of metallic coverage was regarded as safe coverage, and to that I shall refer presently. The notes were part of our authorized and legal note issue, and they became part of the note issue which was taken over by the Bank of Canada and for which it assumed responsibility.
J have given that illustration merely as indicative of what might be done when necessity compels, as it did in 1914. As I read the observations of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence, I certainly concluded that he contemplated the utilization of the national credit in much that way. The Prime Minister had assured me that I was wrong in my conclusion as to that, and I have not joined issue with him on that because, after all, what one man understands from what another man says is not always the test of what one may regard as what was intended by the man who spoke the words.

If he will turn up Hansard he will see what I mean.
