maintopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OF SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
That was what was said anyway.
Now let us go a step further. We have substituted for the provisions to which I have referred a provision with respect to rediscount, and so I get back to what I pointed out at the very start, that when there is no occasion for rediscount, when business conditions are such that there is no opportunity for the banks to use the enormous deposits they have, there is no opportunity for the Bank of Canada to function as a rediscount bank any more
than there would have been for the finance department to function in emitting credit to the banks. That is the first difficulty we must face, and until we can restore the confidence of the people of this country in business we cannot expect this bank to function as a bank of rediscount. It is there; it is on the statute books; we have provided for it; but all you have to do is to look at the statements of the banks to-morrow and you will find that the banks have enormous holdings of our securities.
I want to say this, and I am sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), if he were here, would agree with me. Of course we are getting money on treasury bills cheap.
I remember when we started doing this. We were told we could not do it; that nobody would want to buy our treasury bills. We started in a very modest way; but as there was no demand for money, as the banks were unable to place in profitable loans the money of their depositors, the demand for shortterm treasury bills increased and the rate decreased. It is a bad sign when treasury bills are cheap. The cheaper they are, the less business there is in the country. I remember once watching the upturn of business in London, where they sell treasury bills on an enormous scale, far beyond anything we can appreciate or understand. There was an upturn of business, whereupon the treasury had to pay more money to sell treasury bills. But as money accumulates and is unable to be utilized by those in whose custody it is placed, treasury bills become cheaper and the rate is lower. That is the story. There cannot be any question about it. All one has to do is make himself familiar with the day to day transactions in respect to these matters.
I am hopeful, as I think every man is, that with increasing confidence on the part of the Canadian people in the business of developing their country there will come a greater demand for credit. But that demand will reflect itself in what? In deposits being converted, not into government loans, but into loans to business, to individuals, to factories, to various things of that sort,-and not for capital, either. That is what I think the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) must always keep in mind: the banks do not provide capital. Why? Because they do not know when they will be called upon to honour the cheques of their depositors. The maintenance of that equilibrium between time loans and time deposits, and demand loans and demand deposits, is the basis of all sound banking, and departure from it, by putting bank deposits into capital securities or into long-term loans, means inevitable disaster, as
428S
Bank oj Canada

has been proved in this country on more than one occasion. That is the position which we occupy. Despite all that may be said to the contrary, it just gets down to this. We can by appropriate legislation repeat what was done in 1915. We have, rightly or wrongly, a public opinion as reflected by a universal rule of less metallic coverage behind sound money than existed prior to 1915. There is no legal metallic coverage by statute in Great Britain, but England has more gold behind her currency to-day than she has had for a very long time, possibly more than she ever had. The Bank of England has more gold to-day than ever before; and when you see the bank's return, remember that it values gold at $20.67 an ounce and not at $35. The stabilization fund has absorbed, for the moment at any rate, the difference between $20.67 and $35 per ounce. I cannot speak as to the position this week, but about eight weeks ago there was more gold in the Bank of England behind its currency issue than there had ever been in its history. There is no longer the issue of "Bradburys." That paper money which was established when the war broke out and was called "Bradburys" has been wiped out. All the notes that are issued south of the Tweed are issued by (he Bank of England, and as I have said, these are covered at the moment by a larger deposit of gold than at any other time in the bank's history, although England is off the gold standard.
Our currency to-day is just as sound as it was at the moment of its greatest soundness. Canadian paper money is covered by metal to the same extent or to a greater extent than it has been at any time in our history.

speechtext:
Much more than at some times in our history. There was a time when we had very much more gold than we have now. I was looking at the figures the other night.
That being so, the only question, I repeat, is how we can utilize to the greatest possible extent the credit that springs from the resources over which this country now has control. I do not see any provision in the bill which contemplates any change of policy. I see nothing that contemplates any change in the conduct of the bank. Instead of the $5,000,000 of shares being scattered all over this country, they are going to be lodged in the treasury. Instead of directors who have to hold shares, and who have some sense of financial responsibility, they now are appointees of the government. I would point out how desirable it is to endeavour to realize, as the commis-
sion in Australia stated in its report, that the directors should be representative of all forms of business and that so far as possible the political factor should not be one to be considered. I am not going to repeat the details of the experience which I had in connection with the organization of the Bank of Canada, but I do not think it could have been successfully organized if it had been subject to the continuance of the tremendous pressure that rs described by the one word "patronage"-not the best word, perhaps, to define it. For instance, some people thought that the Bank of Canada should be an institution which at once would provide them with loans of anywhere from $1,000 to $1,000,000. I see that two of my friends opposite nod their heads; they come from rural constituencies, and they were asked on some occasions why they were not able to get money for their electors. I have received many letters of that type.
The Bank of Canada is not at all that sort of institution. It has no accounts of that kind; it reflects its activities and the power of its position only by indirect methods on the banking system of the country. Again I say I can only hope that we may be able to devise some method whereby this great untouched reservoir of credit can be utilized for the public weal. That is the problem before us, just how that can be brought about-on the one hand, to preserve the solvency and reputation of the country; on the other, to utilize to the most the accumulated good will and reputation of the country, which after all is credit. I am not here to solve the problem- it is not my responsibility-but I desire only to point out that great results have followed in some parts of our empire from the efforts which have been made in that direction.
One word more, with respect to the acquisition of the bank. I pointed out in 1936 that if the country desired to take the bank, they should expropriate it and acquire the shares. They have taken the shares now at 120. or a little short of that, and those who sell their shares will have made 41 per cent dividend and 20 per cent profit on their venture, which is not bad in these days.
In New Zealand, if my memory serves me aright, they did not provide so large a profit to those whose shares they took. It was just shortly after the state took over, that I visited New Zealand, and I inquired of the governor of the bank precisely how matters were being worked out. Will the hon. members keep in mind one thing that differentiates us from all these countries and prevents us from making a comparison of the type that I have sometimes made here to-night with the type

Bank oj Canada
that others make. Australia has her debt domiciled in two places only, London and Australia. They did have a small loan in New York, but that is not important at the moment; it was an experiment. New Zealand's debts are domiciled in London and New Zealand, and all sales of produce of New Zealand find payment in sterling lodged in their banks there for the purpose of servicing their debt, paying interest on their debt there. Then, when the exchange is made, the pound, New Zealand and Australia, is practically on a 81 basis with us. One can get some idea, therefore, how it stands with respect to sterling.
It is a purely technical matter how they maintain the exchange rate. The governors of the banks told me how simple it was to maintain it. The suggestion has been made- I remember the Minister of National Defence having made it-that we should have depreciated our dollar. Well, heaven only knows it was depreciated enough by causes over which we had no control without our wanting to depreciate it more; and the gentleman who made representations to the royal commission at Winnipeg, who was not a Canadian, was confronted with the situation that we had a third creditor which these other countries have not. We have the great country to the south of us as our creditor, a country where we owe enormous sums of money, federally, provincially, municipally and by corporations. When England went off the gold standard we still had, in terms of our contract, before the United States took the action they did, to pay our debts there in gold; and having to do so was what brought about the greatest strain that this country has ever had to undergo. Fortunately, with the good will of some of the United States banks and a combination of fortuitous circumstances. we were able to meet every obligation in terms of our contract, and that is the reason that ultimately we were able to restore our credit in face of the difficulties we had to meet.
We must never forget, however, that the action taken by the United States was really the determining factor in changing the picture as a whole. That third factor-not England, not Canada, but those debts in the United States that were payable in gold-was the factor which created such a serious situation in our economy. That difficulty no longer confronts us in the way it did. Why? Because of the action taken by the United States with respect to gold, with respect to paper, with respect to all these matters; and their action has had the effect, of course, of releasing us from a tremendous burden which frankly at
one time it looked as though it might be almost impossible for us to bear. That differentiates our position from that of Australia or New Zealand. They have no such situation as we have.
There is another factor that was mentioned the other day. We have a great favourable commodity balance with Great Britain; we have an adverse balance with the United States; and the utilization of that balance in London to discharge the adverse balance in New York is, of course, the basis of international trade; only you have to multiply it by several ' countries in addition to those; here an adverse balance, and there a favourable balance; the utilization of this favourable balance with respect to that adverse balance, and so on. Largely, however, it was a matter between London and New York. That is a factor which can never be forgotten.

Yes; but I have been
leaving gold out of the question. Gold, becoming a commodity pure and simple as it now is, has made the situation very much belter and simpler for us in every way. To-day gold is a commodity like tobacco or pulpwood or anything of that kind. That is all it is at the moment. There is in the library a book that gives a wonderful history of the reason why gold-has kept the place it has through all the centuries. It is not that it is money alone but that it has always represented something *which in the eyes of all generations has had a peculiar value. It is that it has been very much admired for its beauty and also, because of its rarity, that it has had a value which no other metal has had.
How this problem can be approached without impairing our credit on the one hand and our reputation on the other is a question which I am sure must be engaging the attention of the government in view of the declarations of policy which they so earnestly made before the last election. I am sure that the Macmillan report, which was substituted for the psalms of David by my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence, has become quite worn by much perusal, but a solution of the difficulties has not been found.
I am only going to suggest, as we reach the sections, that thirteen directors are too large a number. There is one other point which I might touch upon. Are we not entitled to have back our bonds now? When the Dominion of Canada handed over to the Bank of Canada various assets we gave them
Bank of Canada

our bonds to guarantee them from responsibility with respect to the assumption of liability for our note issue. Do we contemplate by the language of this bill the transfer of those bonds back to the country? I have looked at it earnestly on more than one occasion, and I am not sure whether it is open to that construction.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the principal matters to which I desire to direct attention.

speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has pointed out, as did the Minister of Finance the other evening, that one of the problems which face the government in the exercise of its control over the currency and credit of the nation is to get into circulation an effective amount of the huge amount of credit and currency that is to-day available. The tremendous amount of credit now available was referred to in a rather indirect way by the Minister of Finance the other evening. I was questioning his statement that the control of the circulation of currency and credit could be exercised through the discount rate and he replied:
I intended to say then just what I am saying now, that the conditions which create that tremendous volume of available credit in all three of these great countries have for the time being rendered any rediscount rate an ineffective weapon. . . .
He was referring to Great Britain, the United States and Canada.
It must be apparent that "that tremendous amount of credit" comes from some direct source, and as a matter of fact, the conditions to which the Minister of Finance referred and which were mentioned indirectly to-night are conditions such as arise when a country abandons gold and goes upon a managed paper standard. Under such conditions the volume of credit is directly under the control of whatever authority is issuing the currency on a managed paper standard. That control has been assumed to be in this government through the Bank of Canada.
Before I go on to deal with that feature, may I point out the extent to which, under the policy of the Conservative party when the Bank of Canada Act was passed and the Bank Act was amended to establish a paper standard, the limits of credit creation were fixed by parliament. In the Bank of Canada reports for May of this year it is disclosed that the total resources are $211,300,000. Of this total $182,300,000 consists of gold, leaving $29,000,000 in foreign currency, mostly United States dollars and pounds sterling. Of the bank's gold holdings only $97,250,000 are

in use as currency reserves leaving $84,850,000 of gold reserves idle and unemployed. That is saying nothing of Canada's annual gold production, from which a substantial increase in that unemployment of gold can be developed. From my own calculations I find that during the last three years, over and above our debt repatriation, payments for goods and all other things, we have exported gold as a commodity to the value of $116,000,000. This means that if there is anything in the Bank of Canada Act with regard to this provision of 25 per cent gold coverage and 5 per cent reserve in the chartered banks, we have actually sabotaged the credit of Canada to the tune of several billion dollars by exporting gold as a commodity, which I think is a serious mistake; for although reserves of gold are being accumulated in England to-day, they are being accumulated not for currency purposes, but for international emergencies, because gold can play a real part in the defensive equipment for the nation.
I estimate that under our Bank of Canada Act we have available to-day a total credit currency of $10,495,000,000. This is made up in this way. Under the Bank of Canada Act the bank may issue four times its gold reserves in Bank of Canada bills, that is, $182,300,000 multiplied by four, or $729,-
200,000.	Against this the bank has issued and has on demand call a total of only $389-
800,000.	This amount subtracted from the total issue authorized by law of $729,200,000 leaves $339,400,000 of Bank of Canada money unissued and unemployed, or sufficient for twenty times that amount in bank deposits, or a total of $6,788,000,000 in bank deposits as provided in subsection 4 of section 59 of the Bank Act. These figures I know are stupendous, but they are within the limits that parliament has fixed for the creation of bank credit currency. Here, then, is the source of some of "that tremendous volume of credit," that the Minister of Finance said made the rediscount rate inapplicable.

speechtext:
In Canada we have this great difference in the banks holdings of currency, as against England. Our banks are allowed to issue their own bank-note currency, which to-day they do to the tune of a hundred million dollars. In other words our banks have, for till money and out-of-pocket transactions of the people, a hundred million dollars of bank-note bills issued by the chartered banks, which the English banks have no privilege of issuing at all.
As a matter of fact, five per cent of Bank of Canada bills is far more than our chartered banks need to carry in their reserve accounts, and that is clearly evidenced by the value of the bank bills they have on deposit with the Bank of Canada, and the value of the Bank
Bank of Canada

of Canada bills which they carry in their actual tills. As a matter of fact, if hon. members will notice, the only amount of Bank of Canada bills that the banks have in their possession for the purpose of meeting public needs, international exchange and interbank transactions, is $53,000,000. The other amount of $194,000,000 they have on deposit with the Bank of Canada. In addition to those combined totals, the Bank of Canada has issued to the people $102,000,000. which amount is to-day circulating in the possession of the people. So that if you will take down the figures you will find that the reserve requirement of 5 per cent is far more than the chartered banks are actually using to-day.
But the point I wish to draw to the attention of the committee is that there is to-day in the possession of the banks $103,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills, against which they can issue $2,060,000,000 of new bank deposits. There is, however, no control in the Bank of Canada or in the government over that $103,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills, which the chartered banks of the dominion own outright. They can use that money if they wish as reserves for new bank deposits, but there is no way by which the government through the Bank of Canada can assert any authority to force them to do so. That Bank of Canada legal tender cash is now being hoarded up by our chartered banks.
It is idle, and though on deposit with the Bank of Canada for the purpose of increasing the nation's currency and credit powers is absolutely under the control of the chartered banks. Let me say again that this does not exhaust the supply of available working capital in Canada, because of the $2,884,000,000 of reported deposits only S6S7,000,003 are on current account; $398,000,000 are on deposit abroad and $1,631,000,000 are in savings accounts. These savings deposits at the present time are drawing on the average not more than one and a half per cent. This means that under this system the banks get the savings of the people as working capital from depositors at one and a half per cent. But that huge amount of money is locked up, as the right hon. the leader of the opposition has pointed out, because nobody has any faith in the future of the country, and nobody is prepared to invest their savings even in government bonds at the present time. Everyone who has a savings bank account knows that this $1,631,000,000 is available for the purchase of government bonds by each owner of the amount to his or her credit in the savings bank account, so that to arrive at the total of Canadian money available for [Mr. McGeer.l
Canadian defence or development, we must add the $1,631,000,000 in the savings accounts to the other amounts I have already mentioned.
Here then is a recapitulation of "the tremendous amount of credit" to use the language of the Minister of Finance, or "the great amount of credit available," to use the language of the right hon. the leader of the opposition, that is now available. The amount available of gold reserves not in use and Bank of Canada bills not issued is $6,798,000,000. The amount which chartered banks may issue on the reserve of Bank of Canada bills not in use, but on deposit with the Bank of Canada, is 82,060,000,000. The amount of savings accounts amounts to $1,631,000,000, or a total of $10,529,000,000.
Under the Bennett monetary policy of 1934 this huge reserve of new currency and credit created by our change in monetary policy was handed over as a public concession to the privately owned Bank of Canada and the privately owned chartered banks. That policy was repudiated in 1935 when the King monetary policy, which declared for "the control of currency issued in terms of public need" and. "to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people," was endorsed from coast to coast.
The issue is no longer inflation; for we in Canada adopted inflation in 1934. The real issue is: Shall our inflated currency and credit be controlled to serve Canada, or shall it remain a concession to Canadian bankers? Surely the answer to that issue must be that Canada's plentiful supply of money should be used for Canadian development, and it must be used to advance and sustain the peace, order, progress, prosperity and security of the Canadian people who are the actual owners of the nation's currency and credit resources.
Any government can grant a concession. Governments have a like power to make concessions so granted valuable by buying back with the taxpayers' money what the concessions yield. It is in the misuse of this authority that democratic governments give way to the oligarchy of privilege, and lose that most important of all things to democratic governments, namely the right to control the great resources of the state in the service of the people. Thus, in the misuse of this authority, democratic governments lose their power, become mere sycophants of monopoly, and wrongly exercise their authority to aid the privileged few in the improper exploitation of the wealth of the state, and of the rights of individuals unable to protect themselves.

Bank of Canada
One of the worst examples of this kind of mistake by democracy is to be found in the Canadian bank policy of 1934, which I hope the present bill aims to cure for under that policy a privately owned bank, the Bank of Canada, was given the exclusive right to issue the full legal tender currency of the Dominion of Canada, which carried with it the right to expand gold into Canadian full legal tender paper money on a basis of one to four. It also gave to the chartered banks the power to use the Bank of Canada not as a national bank but as a mere filling station. Acting in that capacity it has issued free to the chartered banks more Bank of Canada bills than the chartered banks require for their legal reserve purposes. That is. the Bank of Canada was made not an institution of the state, but a mere servant of the chartered banks. Now, when the chartered banks may use Bank of Canada bills by expanding SI Bank of Canada bills into S20 of bank credit money, and exchange that type of money for interest bearing government bonds, it seems to me that we have gone the limit in adopting the course of keeping the government, the state and the people poor, and in making one isolated group in the community rich, by giving it possession of all the money wealth of the nation.
It is an extraordinary thing, but true, that under the policy now in effect the chartered banks can exchange mere bookkeeping entries for government bills bearing interest, and government bonds. But it was in this great concession that some of iis saw one of the great mistakes the Dominion of Canada was making under the Conservative government of 1934.
I came to Ottawa and laid such views before the banking and commerce committee, urging that the Bank of Canada be nationally owned and be made an arm of government to control the issue and circulation of the currency and credit wealth of the nation. It is because we are now coming to the adoption of the very things that were advocated then, and that I advocated in the election of 1935, that I think this parliament under Liberalism is starting on the way to establish a real Canadian democracy and to free the people of the Dominion of Canada from the oligarchy of money power which has dominated it for every year of its existence.
By way of illustrating the evils of this concession which was granted in 1934, and which we in this house I hope are now moving to correct, may I point out that any one of our chartered banks possessed of S5 of Bank of Canada bills can now buy, under the authority of our laws, 8100 of national treasury certificates or government interest bearing
bonds by merely entering in its books a deposit credit in favour of the government. In this way parliament, back in the days of 1934 under the Conservative administration, authorized our chartered banks to issue alleged bank deposits as an effective substitute for Canadian money. The great prerogative of the state, the right to create legal tender and the medium of exchange of the government and the people was then handed over to a private monopoly. Is it any wonder that under such a system the banks have continued to pay their dividends?
Now that our chartered banks are allowed to buy government securities with bookkeeping entries, it should not be surprising to learn on an examination of their books that they own
SI,155,000.000 worth of interest bearing securities issued by our dominion and provincial governments, nor should it be surprising to learn that from 1934, when this concession was granted, until to-day. they have increased their holdings of provincial and dominion government securities by S471.000.000. Every dollar's worth of those securities has been purchased with a bookkeeping entry of alleged bank deposits, which analysis will show, instead of its being a deposit, is merely a practice where the banks are trading short in money and long in credit. That is all it amounts to. That is a service which should be appropriated to the use of the state through its own banking system. But even if the bankers perform that service for the government, they are entitled to a proper service charge, but they are not entitled to charge interest as though they were lending the government their own or their depositors' money.
The vital importance of correcting such a situation should be recognized as imperative once it is realized that if the government securities amounting to $1,155,000,000 now held by the chartered banks carry interest rates on the average of three per cent, the taxpayers are paying the chartered banks S33,-
450,000	a year for merely converting government securities into bank deposits by bookkeeping entries. This bonus of taxpayers' wealth is out of all proportion to the service rendered to the state by the chartered banks. The banks do use debt-free money, and they do use interest-free money through the exercise of parliament's power to create an effective medium of exchange. Could there be a more perfect scheme to make bankers rich and keep the government poor?
This government, by continuing the Conservative policy of 1934, sanctions the vesting in privately owned banks of parliament's power to create and control the issuance of the nation's credit, and to convert it into
Bank of Canada

bankers' bank deposit currency, which is tantamount to the transfer of the government's power to mint money to a private monopoly. The direct result is that both government and people are under the control of men who employ the nation's credit as the stock in trade of the business of making money by manipulating the nation's debt-free money and the nation's interest-free credit. Thus, by our own laws, this parliament has placed mass usury in control of the nation. Under the circumstances we cannot expect balanced budgets, but we should expect unemployment and destitution, stagnation in national development, debt repudiation, confiscatory taxation, municipal and provincial bankruptcy, class and sectional dissension and waning faith in our country's future, because the present Prime Minister has correctly informed this house and the people of the land that "usury once in control will wreck a nation." This is not usury in the ordinary sense; it is mass usury gone mad. It is one reason why this vast country, with its wealth and its future, with its industry and its capacity, stagnates and wallows in a world that is going ahead all about us. I believe we can go forward if we will but manage our national currency and credit in the service of the state.
May I just take one or two minutes to confirm the conclusions I have arrived at from what was undoubtedly a very carefully prepared speech of the hon. Minister of Finance delivered on March 8. On page 2 of the copy of that address which has been circulated, he acknowledged that bank deposits created by bookkeeping entries in the books of our chartered banks are being substituted for money by saying:
As every one knows the story of the last century ... is a story of the general rise of bank deposits to perform the monetary work of the business world.
"And," he should; have added, "the monetary work of the government world," because our governments now use cheques transferring bank deposits in the place of money, as does everyone else. He then referred to the power of the chartered banks to expand Bank of Canada bills into alleged bank deposits. At page 3 he said:
Speaking .of the banks as a whole, the proportion or percentage of cash which the banks keep is in practice about ten per cent, and by law it must be at least five per cent. . .	.
Suppose, for example, that the Bank of Canada buys $10,000,000 worth of securities. Then, no matter from whom it buys those securities, the reserves of the chartered banks as a whole will rise by the amount of $10,000,000.
[Mr. McGeer.l
Then, after explaining that this was an example of open market operation and presenting some details to prove that proposition, he went on to say:
Thus it is that the security purchases by the Bank of Canada tend to expand bank deposits in the country by approximately ten times the amount of the transaction.
Or, in a word, whenever the Bank of Canada issues $10,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills to buy gold or government securities, the law gives to the chartered banks the power to issue $200,000,000 of chartered bank buying power in bank deposit money in the form of alleged bank deposits. However, the banks, as the Minister of Finance points out, have allegedly overruled the law of parliament and instead of expanding bank credit on a 5 per cent cash reserve basis, they profess to have increased the reserves held to 10 per cent, which, of course, if a true statement, would reduce the amount of bank deposits authorized by parliament on a reserve of $10,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills to the $100,000 000 the minister mentioned. Then the minister went on to explain just how the chartered banks could use that $100,000,000 of bank deposit money to purchase government bills and interest bearing bonds. At this point he said:
You may ask just how the chartered banks will expand their assets and deposits as a result of open market operations by the Bank of Canada. If the chartered banks can find good borrowers they will tend to increase their ordinary commercial loans, and by so doing increase their deposit liabilities by a similar amount. Otherwise they may buy investment securities which will usually earn them a considerably lower rate, or they may expand partly in one way and partly in the other. Either move will increase the aggregate of deposits of the banking system as a whole.
Now investment securities are government bonds. Therefore, when the Bank of Canada issues $10,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills under our banking laws, the chartered banks are empowered to create $200,000,000 in bank deposits which may be exchanged for treasury bills or any other form of interest-bearing government bonds. So, on the authority of the Minister of Finance, we find that parliament has authorized the chartered banks to create their own buying power with a bookkeeping system which they use to buy government bonds. The bankers thus use the tremendous volume of credit, created by our managed currency system, for which they do not pay interest. It offers a splendid illustration of what we call orthodox finance. It

Bank o/ Canada
is one of the most dangerous concessions that has ever been issued by a democratic government to private capital.
I know that a long time is going to elapse between the time we establish national ownership of the Bank of Canada and the time when we shall have the fruits of a really national currency policy. But we are on the way. Just as men must know that they cannot run their homes without money and could not run them if those unfriendly to them controlled their money resources, we in government must come to recognize that government cannot afford to be out of control of the nation's currency and credit. I grant that there will come much heavier responsibilites upon government in the administration of a managed currency system where there is no longer the security of the restricted nineteenth century gold standard system. There will be public demands and temptations to overcome, but the standard of intelligence of government to-day is a little different from what it was in John Law's time, or two hundred years or more ago. The problems of managed currency and credit that face us to-day belong to the twentieth century, and it is because they are of the twentieth century that twentieth century democratic government must rise superior to the challenge that these problems present. We cannot go on in the midst of opportunity, worshipping a' the shrine of things that are obsolete and ignoring the opportunities for progress that exist. We must find the practical and effective way to finance progress.
I would say that with the establishment of the national ownership of the Bank of Canada we should be able to meet the problem put up to this committee by the leader of the opposition to-night, namely, that of finding a way with this huge reserve of managed currency at our disposal, to put into circulation the funds necessary to give security and peace and order and progress and the production and the use of wealth to Canada and the Canadian people. How can that be done?
With this enormous credit wealth under the control of government, we can reestablish the social services of this dominion, modelling ours along the line of the British plan. I would say that we could greatly improve and extend our old age pension system into a much more generous and Christian practice than it is to-day. Possibly we can adopt the sixty year limit, as the leader of the opposition advocated during the election of 1935. We can give definite aid in unemployment insurance and health service programs, and take 51952-272
from the overburdened provinces and municipalities the cost of unemployment relief. We can give contributions in aid of financing needy mothers and children, and contributions in aid of education, which needs to be brought up to twentieth century standards. We can give contributions to the provinces and municipalities for the maintenance of law and order. We can aid in the protection of those who suffer from physical disability, which lessens their capacity for gainful employment. We can do all these things if we will only recognize that we are no longer poor. We can give grants in aid, as Great Britain is doing, for municipal reconstruction and expansion. If these things can be done in Great Britain and other European countries, why cannot we with all our wealth do them? We can improve our urban and rural housing. We can aid in the promotion of better health in the dominion. We can create health centres, gymnasia, amphitheatres equipped with effective health, recreation, and educational facilities.
We can develop our tourist trade. The leader of the opposition has said that we have to meet our national obligations in the United States. No more effective way could be found than in the development of our tourist trade. A great national highway system could be developed, including the building of truly modern highways from all the gateway points on the international boundary line, leading northward to Canadian cities and to our tourist attractions. The beautification of our cities and countryside would give employment and new life to the dominion, and we should give special attention to the commemoration of many places of historical interest, and our unemployed should be at work developing tourist accommodation around Canada's many places of scenic beauty and natural wonder.
National defence is a thing we cannot ignore. We should develop the production at home as far as is practical of every conceivable form of equipment and accoutrement required in the services.
Probably the time has come when we should have a vigorous campaign to reestablish loyalty on the part of Canadian youth to our Canadian country and democratic government, under our constitutional sovereign.
The passage of this bill will mark one of the great milestones in the economic life of Canadian civilization. It is not a step that is going to be retraced. If it is followed with a national currency policy that will put into effect the declarations and promises which the Liberal party made in 1935, we shall have a

Bank of Canada

new Canada, a Canada of a happy and united people, a Canada that will be worthy of everything that the fathers of confederation dreamed we would accomplish in the future.
We lack one thing and one thing only- the means of financing Canadian progress, and with the establishment of national ownership of the Bank of Canada that now comes to us. It will make us not only a happy and united people but something more. It will give us the right to stand forth as a nation on the North American continent, worthy of the traditions of the two great races from which we came, playing our part in partnership with other nations to do something not only for the development of ourselves but for the good of the world that is sadly in need of the kind of leadership which we of the British empire should offer.
I venture to say that if we will look forward to cooperating in the great celebration that is going to take place in the United States next year, when our neighbours celebrate the 150th anniversary of their nation's birth, we can make a contribution to world peace that will be worth while. If. for instance, we were able to induce an international exchange of courtesies that would come to pass with a visit of His Imperial Majesty the King of England and his gracious queen to the north American continent next year, a visit that would include both Canada and the United States, we would be doing something that would send a message of good will throughout all the world! When we realize what is taking place under the tripartite agreement and the very many obligations of France and England to-day, we should, as we pass this bill, dedicate ourselves to something more than a consideration of merely Canadian affairs. Let me say that in our world the progress of human enlightenment. bringing in its wake a more generous measure-

I just want to say a few words in conclusion. I have studied finance in theory for something over seventeen years. I have had the privilege of sitting in provincial houses and in the executive offices of council chambers, and in all these places I have never known the time in the public life of this dominion when the problem of financing was not the greatest difficulty of government. Every man who has ever been charged with the responsibility of public affairs has found
rMr. McGeer.)
himself face to face with this difficulty. Things that should have been done, things that should have been improved, could not be done or could not be improved because the public authority did not have the money. I think one of the greatest handicaps of democracy has been the apparent refusal of public men to study the problems of practical public finance. They have been treated as something akin to the weather, something over which we had no control, something we did not have the capacity to understand. I sat in the gallery and heard two ministers of finance, being introduced to their chairs, proclaiming the fact that they did not know anything about money; that they never hoped to know anything about money, and that for that reason they expected to be good ministers of finance. Of course that attitude is silly, because our financial institution does not come from on high; it is man-made in every particular of its machination, and every law that has been passed by any parliament or other lawmaking authority at the behest of the financial world has always proven pernicious to posterity and disastrous in the end. For that reason I say that with the nationalization of the Bank of Canada we are moving to a new day for humanity. But I want to confess that in our world the progress of human enlightenment, bringing in its wake more generous measures of human service and wider understanding of social justice, spirals upwards with disheartening slowness.
Old habits of thought, old customs and old-established institutions die hard, if they die at all. Loyalty to the things we know and fear of the new help even bad institutions to persist long after their disturbing and baneful influence is acknowledged by common agreement. Such institutions, particularly those born of self-interest, never die at all, and it seems that they pass away only when we mix the blood of life and the sweat of toil together in the tragedy of death-dealing revolution and war. Yet it is a world in which we cannot lose faith; for its histor}' and tradition, its present and its future, lend it a baffling dignity that inspires us with the nobility of service even in the moments of our greatest trials and defeats.
Ineffectiveness, the handmaiden of impatience, will at times lead us into paths of intolerance and indulgence-those treacherous twin demon offspring of despairing futility. But if we will always remember that while men come and go like bubbles on a stream, a worthy idea once sown in the social consciousness of a people will in time bear good fruit and live on forever, and the will to do

Bank of Canada
well in public service is not likely to perish. If our faith in the destiny of our country is good and true, we are certain to find encouraging consolation even in those irritating delays and disappointing reverses which we ought to know are the steadying and essential punctuation marks of timely and orderly progress. I look upon the nationalization of the Bank of Canada as something of real encouragement.
Yes, I have taken time to-night to put a few moments on some things I wanted to say. I for one believe that Canada can be rebuilt. It is my hope and wish that it will be rebuilt under the kind of leadership which the Liberal government of the day, through its capacity, gained from long years of experience in Canadian affairs, has to offer. The reconstruction of Canada is bound to come. In my humble opinion it will be better if it comes under experienced Liberalism than in any other form. That this Liberal government is now taking upon itself the great responsibility of administering the nation's currency and credit as a public utility in the service of the nation and its people is an indication that the Liberalism of Canada is keeping pace with the progress of the twentieth century. I for one have only one desire, and that is to lend to this government and to the Liberal party whatever service I may have to offer to help to make this government a truly democratic government, serving Canada with all the power and means that the government of Canada has within its power to advance every section of our nation and to help every class of our Canadian people.

I have been amazed, as have most hon. members, at statements made this evening. The chartered banks owe:
Their shareholders for the sums they have put into the enterprise;
Their customers the amount of their deposits, payable either on demand or on notice.
To meet those liabilities the banks own buildings, cash, loans and government securities. In no case, by any legerdemain, can a bank ever have government or other securities in excess of its deposits. And if hon. members will take the trouble to look at the returns of the chartered banks, they will find that deposits are liabilities on their balance sheets and not assets.

If an elector applies to have his or her name placed on the list, or if the enumerators place a name on the list, it should be placed on the list for the polling division, which I assume is the polling section, in which that person resides. There is no doubt about it.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
That is all right. When we considered the matter the debate ran something like this, that an elector might at a general revision be placed on the list for a particular polling section or division, as it is called here; then the same lists would be the lists for a subsequent by-election. If there had been removal in the meantime of the elector from one polling section to another in the same electoral division, then under subsection 3 of section 16 that elector could vote in the polling section in which he was registered, although in the meantime he may have removed to another polling section in the division.
But certainly it seems to me there can be no objection to the fact that an elector is registered for the polling division in which he ordinarily resides. If you change it, it means this, that, although not ordinarily residing in the polling division, an elector may be placed upon a list in a polling division five or ten or fifty miles away from the place where he resides, in which there can be no supervision over his identity, and no neighbours who know as to whether or not he is properly on the list.
But if, when the general revision of the lists takes place before a general election, he is entered on the lists for the polling division in which he resides, and then subsequently, before the next by-election, moves into another polling division in the same electoral district, then subsection 3 of section 16 preserves his right to vote. It seems to me that if you make a change you are complicating matters very much.

And we only ask that we go back to the law as it was in force prior to the changes made in 1934. The hon. member says there would be no supervision about his being put on the list. Certainly there is supervision. If his name is placed on the list in a logging camp, there is a rural registrar there who knows every man in the camp. It may be a small community not exceeding a hundred people altogether, and certainly the registrar, w'ho is generally the bookkeeper, is in a thorough position to know whether a person is entitled to be put on or not. The fact that he is there is evidence of that portion of it.
As I say, we are only asking to go back to the conditions which existed before. Much attention has been directed to the words "ordinarily resident" in the Dominion of Canada and in the electoral district. But I should like to emphasize the fact that there are three conditions imposed. One is that he must be ordinarily resident in Canada. We are not proposing to interfere with that at all. The second is that he must be ordinarily resident in the electoral district. We are not proposing to interfere with that at all either, although I would like to. We only ask that he be allowed to be registered in the polling division in which he is then living.
The other night I gave an illustration of North Vancouver, which is part rural and part urban. A man has his wife there. The term

"ordinarily resident" is interpreted, according to section 16, to mean the place where he has his wife and family. When you get duplication, you have the door open for personation and for double voting.

speechtext:

section 14, subsection 1 of the bill, everybody would come in under the exceptions as cited in section 16-clergymen,	teachers and
students. Where they are really resident in two places they have the option. I am sure that was not the object or purpose of the committee.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
I moved the amendment
only in order to try to meet the wishes of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who seemed to have made out a fairly good case. If, as appears, the committee is almost unanimously against it, I am quite willing to withdraw the amendment.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member sitting behind me said that this might come in under the provisions of section 16. I would be quite agreeable if he would kindly insert " miner, logger, fisherman and seaman " along with " clergyman, teacher and student." That is what I am objecting to. It is class legislation. You let these three classes in under exactly similar conditions, or rather with fewer qualifications. To hon. members who are so afraid of a man from one electoral district voting in another let me say we are not asking for that, but under the provisions of section 16 a minister, a teacher or a pupil can vote not only in another polling division but in another electoral district. We are not asking for that. We shall be satisfied if you will allow these classes I have mentioned to vote only under circumstances where they are living in the same electoral district but have moved into another polling division. Some of the explanations are down at the bottom of the page and some are at the top of the next page. This is the way the old act would read if the word " ordinarily," was left out. We will just take it out and see if there is any objection as we go along: " Every person shall be qualified to vote in the polling division in which he resides at the time of the preparation of the list "[DOT]-that is after the issue of the writ-"if"-these are the conditions-"(a) he is twenty-one years old, (b) a British subject, and (c) has been ordinarily "-we will leave that word there-[DOT]" resident in Canada for the twelve months immediately preceding polling day," and "(d) was ordinarily resident in the electoral district at the date of the issue of the writ." Those are the conditions when, even with the word " ordinarily" removed, a man could register only in the polling division in which he was then living. That was the old act. It worked well before; why should it not act now? If you strike out these men, you are going to disfranchise-one of the hon. members for Vancouver contradicted me when I said twenty per cent would be disfranchised; he said, more than that. From
Elections and Franchise

my knowledge of conditions I suggest that if you are going to disfranchise those men you will kindly disfranchise the parson and the teacher and the student as well. We will treat them all alike if you are going to treat these men on a bad basis.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman, in view of section 16, subsection 1, explain how you disfranchise them?

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Because when a man goes to register in a logging camp, let us say, the man there says to him, " I would be glad to put you on; you have been here since the day of the issue of the writ, but I have to follow the wording of the act, which says ' ordinarily resident,' and according to section 16 your home is the place to which you intend to return."

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: And how far would the logging camp be from the home?

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Three hundred miles.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: It might be two hundred miles. Section 16 says " ordinarily resident ": the place of his habitation or home whereto, when away therefrom, he intends to return. He does intend to return. The man could be registered by the one who employs him or by a brother employee who knows he is on the paylist. I do not see how any corruption could occur, and the best proof is that it has not taken place, at least in British Columbia.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member for Comox-Alberni how this example I am going to give would be taken care of if the word " ordinarily " is left out. I have in mind a family who lived in Uxbridge, Ontario. The head of the house worked during the election away up in northern Ontario, that is the northern part of the riding of Ontario, perhaps a hundred miles away from home.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: The same electoral district?

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: The same electoral district. His wife, naturally, registered him at the home in Uxbridge, because he was away only for a few months working on roads in Muskoka, and he was also registered where he worked up in Muskoka. Therefore his name is on both lists. How could you prevent him from voting in both places? How would you prevent impersonation?

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
The only place where he
could vote would be the place where he was. He would not be put on at his home town.

speechtext:
I do not want to take
up the time of the committee, but I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has overlooked an essential difference between the case we are considering and that of a clergyman. The case we are considering under this section is based upon the fact that there is no change of residence, for the man is a resident of the electoral district all the time. But in the case of the clergyman, the school teacher and the others to whom he has referred there has been an actual change of residence. These men have gone out of one constituency into another and have thereby lost any right to vote. It is for that reason that there is a saving clause in connection with cases of that kind.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
In order to give them the
vote?

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, because they have
lost it, because they have changed their residence.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: So has my man.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: No, he has not. That is just the difference. He is still a resident of the electoral district. The hon. member's whole argument is based on the contention that his man is still a resident of the electoral district. Therefore he has not lost his vote as the clergyman and the teacher and the others referred to have lost their votes, through having moved into another constituency. That is why there is a special provision to take care of them.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
Yes. The only difference is that the ease made by the hon. member for Leeds is a great deal worse. He wants to give the vote to men of the classes he mentions when they have moved to another electoral district altogether. We only say that the man should be allowed to vote at another polling division when he is living in the same electoral district. According to the hon. member's argument, if you allow it in his case you must allow it with greater force in mine. The primary object should be to give every man a vote, and that is why the parson is allowed to be reregistered in an electoral district into which be has moved. We are not going as far as that, but we are satisfied to say that as long as a man remains in the same electoral district he should be given a chance to vote in the polling division in which he resides. The hon. member for Leeds says that he has not forfeited his right to vote in the place where he started from, but he is prevented, because a poor working man cannot afford to go back 100 or 150 miles to vote. It would

Elections and Franchise
cost him $25 and he would lose his job. The question is, Do we or do we not want to have him vote. Do we want the proletariat, a word so often abused, to have a chance to vote? I know a good many of these men would vote against me, and I do not intend to run again, anyhow. I am merely fighting for the general principle. We fought this matter out ten years ago; the provision was made, and no harm came of it. A couple of thousand people in British Columbia alone will be affected.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: We wish every man to have a vote; but the committee has taken strong ground against permitting one man to have two votes, one man to be entered twice on the list, so that he can vote in one place himself, and offer facilities for somebody else to impersonate him where his name is on the other list. That is the evil we have to meet.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: What is in the mind of the law? Who is going to establish the ordinary residence of an elector? The elector himself, I submit. Even if he is temporarily absent from the real, ordinary residence of his family, and if he informs the officer that the other place where he lived is his ordinary residence, who will condemn him for having so declared and for voting there, even though, with the words "ordinarily resident," his family are allowed to have his name registered in his absence? I do not see much difference.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
I rise to support the
amendment, and the arguments in favour of it put forward by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. In British Columbia we have recognized for the past twenty-five years that there were a great many people entitled to vote who could not vote on election day where they ordinarily reside. That is, in the polling division or even in the electoral district where they live. As a matter of fact, the amendment, although it helps some, will not make it possible for a great many in British Columbia to vote. We have miners, loggers, fishermen and sailors who go away from their homes for six, seven, eight or nine months, and they may be away on election day. We shall have to find some means whereby these people can vote, if elections are to have any meaning to them at all. What is the use of talking about democracy and democratic methods to a man who cannot vote on election day? That is what these men will say. They will tell you. "I have been in this province for so many years and have not yet been able to cast a vote." As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pointed out. if we have made provision for teachers and preachers to vote, why not make provision for more useful people to vote, the people who do the world's work?

In the last federal act we were able to have it included in a partial way, but we were told that there was the question of expense. There was a cost of so many dollars per vote.

speechtext:
Yes; I have known of votes that were cheaper and votes that were dearer than that. I am satisfied that it would not cost half that if the officials carrying on the election were properly instructed. I submit that this committee, if they are going to attach any value whatever to elections, will have to find ways by which people who are away from home on election day, and indeed for months before and months after that day, can exercise their franchise.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I support the remarks of
the hon. member for Comox-AIberni and the hon. member for Vancouver East. In the constituency which I represent in British Columbia, if there were an election right now, there would be from four to five hundred men who would not have a vote. That condition should not obtain, and I think it can be remedied. The hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George is fearful that some fellow may vote twice. I think it is far more injurious to democracy for one man to be deprived of his vote than for some fellow to have voted twice. After all, there is a law that protects us, and if a man votes twice he can be sent to penitentiary. That is a consideration which will restrain most men.

speechtext: It was with a view to obtaining peace and making a certain amount of progress that I moved the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Comox-AIberni. Perhaps we could settle our difficulties 'if we had a division. Personally, I am willing to vote for the amendment, which I moved merely as a matter of compromise. If we have a vote, I think we shall get on a little faster.

subtopic: MEASITHE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
Does the minister not think that if we slept over it to-night, better thoughts might prevail to-morrow? Suppose we allow it to stand and go on to some of the
Elections and Franchise

other sections? When hon. members read in Hansard the report of these proceedings they will appreciate the situation and they may take a different view. The hon. member for Vancouver East very properly raised the point that it should apply also to the electoral district. If we are to have a scrap, let us have a substantial one, and that would meet the objection of the hon. member for New Westminster as well. That was our ambition to begin with. For the sake of peace we gave away a third of our birthright, and we are satisfied to accept this condition that it should apply only to the polling division within the electoral district. That was going a very long way out of our way; and as the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) says, Why should men be disfranchised? If we are going to make provision for people away from home as we have done in section 16, for the parson-I have every respect for the parson- and the teacher and the student, why should we not make provision for the sailor and the farmer and the logger and people of that kind, especially when we want it done only inside the electoral district, whereas these others are going to get the privilege of moving from one electoral district to another? There is no doubt that paragraphs (c) and (d) of section 14 are ancillary-I do not think that is the word-are a condition of the words used in subsection 1, which states:
Save as hereinafter provided every person, man or woman, shall be qualified to vote and be entitled to be registered as an elector on the list of electors for the polling division in which he or she ordinarily resides-*
Or "resides," if justice prevailed.
-at the time of the preparation and revision of the list of electors therefor if-
Now "if" means there is a condition attached. There happen to be quite a number.
-he or she
(a)	is of the full age of twenty-one years or will attain the full age of twenty-one years on or before polling day at the pending election ; and-
This is another condition:
(b)	is a British subject by birth or naturalization : and
Here is a further condition:
(c)	has been ordinarily resident in Canada for the twelve months immediately- preceding polling day at the pending election; and
That covers the provision about ordinary residence in Canada, and (d) deals with the electoral district:
(d)	-was ordinarily resident in the electoral district at the date of the issue of the writ for the pending election; and at a by-election has continued to be ordinarily resident therein until polling day.

The word "ordinarily" is allowed there. That ties him down to the electoral district. The amendment comes in only as regards the polling division. The effect will be as it was in 1930; ordinarily resident in Canada, ordinarily resident in the electoral district and resident in the polling division. I might quote the affidavit, form 45 to illustrate. That has been in force ever since I have been in politics I think:
Oath of person whose name is not on the official list of electors for a rural polling division and who is qualified to vote.
(sec. 46)
(1)	You swear (or affirm) that you are a British subject of the full age of twenty-one years; that you have been ordinarily resident in Canada for the last twelve months and that you were ordinarily resident in this electoral
district on the	day of	 19..
(naming the date of the issue of the writ of election) ; (and, at a by-election, you have continued to be ordinarily resident in this electoral district until to-day).
He has to take that oath, so it is fully protected.
(2)	That you now reside in this polling division.
That form has been like that since 1921; they only had to take the oath that they " now reside " in this polling division. Why we should change it at this date. I do not know.
(3)	That you are not within any of the classes of persons who lack qualification or are disqualified by reason of appointment to judicial office, employment in this electoral district for pay or reward in reference to the pending election, race, crime, mental incapacity or disfranchisement for corrupt or illegal practices;
(4)	That you have not received anything nor has anything been promised to you directly or indirectly, in order to induce you to vote or to refrain from voting at this election; and
(5)	That you have not already voted at this election or been guilty of any corrupt or illegal practice in relation thereto. So help you God.
Then there is a note that when the elector is a clergyman, teacher, pupil or summer resident, there will, at his request, be substituted for the first paragraph of this oath the appropriate alternative. That shows that it was originally intended, and has been all down the years since 1921 at any rate, that they were to be given the opportunity of voting in the polling division in which they then reside. I call attention to the fact that the explanation offered on the page opposite page 60 reads as follows:
Section 46. No change. At present these provisions appear in s. 46A of the act.

Seeds Act
That is, to put it mildly, a false statement, and possibly led some members of the committee to agree to the insertion of this word " ordinarily," because they looked and said, " Oh this is the same as it was before; there is no change." It is not the same as it was before, because the word " ordinarily " has been put in and it changes it substantially. I would not be surprised if that influenced the members in the committee, because on Friday when we were going through this bill and came to a section and read the explanation " no change," someone said, " Carried," and it went right through. But where it said there has been a change, someone wanted an explanation and the thing was threshed out. There is the no doubt inadvertent misstatement that there is no change. There has been a change. All we are asking is that the provision be left as it was before. It might be possible to put in an amendment to the effect-as it seems to be inimical to our good friends from Quebec rather than the west- that it apply only to British Columbia and possibly the northern part of Ontario, because there must be similar conditions there. I am sorry we have not heard from hon. members from that section. I was hoping to hear from the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor), because I think his district contains similar conditions.
